title: Ἄϋπνος νύξ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Book 20 opens in the vestibule of the house, where Odysseus lies on an oxhide and fleeces, awake and thinking of vengeance. The maids who sleep with the suitors go laughing out of the hall, and his heart growls like a dog guarding her puppies; he strikes his chest and tells his heart to endure, as it once endured the Cyclops. Athena stands over his head, in the likeness of a woman. He tells her his fear: he is one against many, and even if he kills them, where could he flee? She answers that she is a god and has guarded him through every labour, and sends him to sleep. Upstairs Penelope wakes, weeps, and prays to Artemis for a sudden death, recalling the daughters of Pandareus who were carried off by the storm-winds. She tells of a dream in which a figure like Odysseus lay beside her. At dawn Odysseus hears her weeping, imagines that she already knows him, puts away his bedding, and lifts his hands in prayer to Zeus.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐν προδόμῳ εὐνάζετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: autar ho en prodomōi eunazeto dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: But he in the fore-house was laying himself down to sleep, heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus was lying down to sleep in the vestibule.
sentences.n: Book 20 turns from Penelope, who has just cried herself to sleep upstairs, back to Odysseus. αὐτὰρ ὁ is 'but he': ὁ is a pronoun here, not the article. προδόμῳ is the 'fore-house', the vestibule at the front of the house. εὐνάζετο is the imperfect middle of εὐνάζω 'put to bed', so in the middle 'was laying himself down to sleep'. δῖος 'heavenly' is Odysseus’s stock epithet and is rendered 'heavenly' every time.

sentences.t:
κὰμ μὲν ἀδέψητον βοέην στόρεσ’, αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
κώεα πόλλ’ ὀΐων, τοὺς ἱρεύεσκον Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr:
kam men adepsēton boeēn stores’, autar hyperthe
kōea poll’ oïōn, tous hireueskon Achaioi·
sentences.l:
Down indeed an untanned oxhide he spread, and on top
many fleeces of sheep, which the Achaeans used to sacrifice;
sentences.i: He spread out an untanned oxhide, and on top of it many fleeces from the sheep that the Achaeans used to sacrifice.
sentences.n: κὰμ μὲν … στόρεσ’ is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: κατά is part of the verb and 'spread down', with κὰμ for κατά before μ. στόρεσ’ is the aorist of στόρνυμι 'spread' with the augment missing and the final -ε elided; the subject is Odysseus, carried over from line 1. ἀδέψητον 'untanned' is ἀ- 'not' + δεψέω 'tan'; βοέην is the feminine of the adjective 'of an ox', used as a noun for the hide. ὕπερθε 'on top'. κώεα 'fleeces' is the plural of κῶας, and ὀΐων the genitive plural of ὄϊς 'sheep'. ἱρεύεσκον: the suffix -σκ- gives a past tense of habit, 'used to', and ἱρεύω is 'sacrifice, slaughter'. Ἀχαιοί is the poem’s name for the Greeks, here the people of Ithaca.

sentences.t: Εὐρυνόμη δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπὶ χλαῖναν βάλε κοιμηθέντι.
sentences.tr: Eurynomē d’ ar’ epi chlainan bale koimēthenti.
sentences.l: And Eurynome then upon him a cloak threw, to him gone to sleep.
sentences.i: And when he had gone to sleep, Eurynome threw a cloak over him.
sentences.n: Eurynome is a woman of the household who appeared in Book 19. ἐπὶ … βάλε is tmesis again, 'threw over'; βάλε is the aorist without augment (Attic ἔβαλε). χλαῖναν is a heavy cloak, and the same word is rendered 'cloak' wherever it occurs. κοιμηθέντι is the aorist passive participle of κοιμάω 'put to sleep', in the dative: 'for him, having been laid to sleep'. ἄρ’ is ἄρα 'then'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς μνηστῆρσι κακὰ φρονέων ἐνὶ θυμῷ
κεῖτ’ ἐγρηγορόων·
sentences.tr:
enth’ Odyseus mnēstērsi kaka phroneōn eni thymōi
keit’ egrēgoroōn·
sentences.l:
There Odysseus, for the suitors evil thinking in his heart,
lay awake;
sentences.i: There Odysseus lay awake, meaning evil for the suitors in his heart.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is 'there'. Ὀδυσεύς has one σ here and two in line 1: the spelling of the name varies with the needs of the verse. κακὰ φρονέων is 'meaning evil', literally 'thinking evil things', with the dative μνηστῆρσι 'for the suitors'. θυμῷ is 'heart': in this part θυμός, κραδίη, ἦτορ and κῆρ are all 'heart' (θυμός is 'life' once, in line 62, and the note there says so), and where two stand close together the note says which is which. κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο, the imperfect of κεῖμαι 'lie'. ἐγρηγορόων is a participle of the perfect ἐγρήγορα 'I am awake', with the epic uncontracted ending -όων.

sentences.t:
ταὶ δ’ ἐκ μεγάροιο γυναῖκες
ἤϊσαν, αἳ μνηστῆρσιν ἐμισγέσκοντο πάρος περ,
ἀλλήλῃσι γέλω τε καὶ εὐφροσύνην παρέχουσαι.
sentences.tr:
tai d’ ek megaroio gynaikes
ēïsan, hai mnēstērsin emisgeskonto paros per,
allēlēisi gelō te kai euphrosynēn parechousai.
sentences.l:
and those women out of the hall
were going, who with the suitors used to mingle as before,
to one another laughter and merriment providing.
sentences.i: And the women who used to lie with the suitors, as they had done before, were going out of the hall, giving one another laughter and merriment.
sentences.n: ταὶ is the feminine plural of the 'article', here a plain demonstrative, 'those' women of the house. ἤϊσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go' (Attic ᾖσαν), 'were going'; ἐκ μεγάροιο 'out of the hall' has the genitive in -οιο. αἵ is the relative 'who', with an accent that tells it from the article αἱ. ἐμισγέσκοντο: the suffix -σκ- makes a past tense of habit, 'used to', and μίσγομαι 'mingle' is used of sleeping with someone. πάρος περ is 'as before'. γέλω is the accusative of γέλως 'laughter' in its Ionic form; ἀλλήλῃσι is the feminine dative plural 'to one another'; παρέχουσαι 'providing'.

sentences.t: τοῦ δ’ ὠρίνετο θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι·
sentences.tr: tou d’ ōrineto thymos eni stēthessi philoisi·
sentences.l: And of him was stirred the heart within his dear breast;
sentences.i: His heart was stirred within his own breast.
sentences.n: τοῦ is the genitive of the pronoun, 'of him', and goes with θυμός: 'his heart'. ὠρίνετο is the imperfect passive of ὀρίνω 'stir up, set in commotion'. στήθεσσι is the dative plural of στῆθος 'breast' in -εσσι; the plural is poetic for the singular. φίλοισι 'dear' is the word Homer uses for what belongs to a person, so the English layer says 'his own'.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ μερμήριζε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
ἠὲ μεταΐξας θάνατον τεύξειεν ἑκάστῃ,
ἦ ἔτ’ ἐῷ μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισι μιγῆναι
ὕστατα καὶ πύματα, κραδίη δέ οἱ ἔνδον ὑλάκτει.
sentences.tr:
polla de mermērize kata phrena kai kata thymon,
ēe metaïxas thanaton teuxeien hekastēi,
ē et’ eōi mnēstērsin hyperphialoisi migēnai
hystata kai pymata, kradiē de hoi endon hylaktei.
sentences.l:
And much he pondered in mind and in heart,
whether, rushing after them, he should contrive death for each,
or yet allow them to mingle with the overweening suitors
for the last and final time; and his heart within him barked.
sentences.i: He pondered long in his mind and heart whether to rush at them and contrive death for each woman, or to let them lie with the overweening suitors one more time, the last and final time; and all the while his heart barked within him.
sentences.n: Odysseus is in two minds, and the Greek gives the two courses as alternatives, ἠέ … ἦ 'whether … or'. πολλά is 'much', an adverb. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is the fixed phrase 'in mind and in heart'. μεταΐξας is the aorist participle of μεταΐσσω 'dart after'. τεύξειεν is the aorist optative of τεύχω 'contrive, bring about', and ἐῷ the subjunctive of ἐάω 'allow', both in the question he puts to himself; ἑκάστῃ is feminine, 'each woman'. ὑπερφιάλοισι is the stock epithet of the suitors, 'overweening'. ὕστατα καὶ πύματα are neuter plurals used as adverbs, 'for the last and final time'. κραδίη is the 'heart' as the seat of anger, and ὑλάκτει is the imperfect of ὑλακτέω 'bark': the verb prepares the dog of the simile.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ κύων ἀμαλῇσι περὶ σκυλάκεσσι βεβῶσα
ἄνδρ’ ἀγνοιήσασ’ ὑλάει μέμονέν τε μάχεσθαι,
ὥς ῥα τοῦ ἔνδον ὑλάκτει ἀγαιομένου κακὰ ἔργα·
sentences.tr:
hōs de kyōn amalēisi peri skylakessi bebōsa
andr’ agnoiēsas’ hylaei memonen te machesthai,
hōs rha tou endon hylaktei agaiomenou kaka erga·
sentences.i: As a dog standing over her tender puppies barks at a man she does not know and is bent on fighting, so his heart barked within him, indignant at those evil deeds;
sentences.n: The comparison opens with ὡς δέ and closes with a second ὥς, 'so': the heart growling in anger is like a mother dog guarding her young. κύων is 'dog' and is feminine here. βεβῶσα is the perfect participle of βαίνω, which with περί means 'standing astride, standing over' (περί is separated from it, tmesis). ἀμαλῇσι … σκυλάκεσσι are datives plural, 'tender puppies' (σκύλαξ). ἀγνοιήσασ’ is the aorist participle of ἀγνοιέω 'fail to recognise'. μέμονε is the perfect of μέμονα 'be eager', with an infinitive. In the last line ὑλάκτει has no stated subject, which is the heart of line 13; τοῦ … ἀγαιομένου is a genitive 'he being indignant' (ἀγαίομαι 'be indignant at'), with κακὰ ἔργα 'evil deeds' as its object.

sentences.t: στῆθος δὲ πλήξας κραδίην ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: stēthos de plēxas kradiēn ēnipape mythōi·
sentences.l: And his chest having struck, his heart he rebuked with a word:
sentences.i: Then he struck his chest and rebuked his heart in these words:
sentences.n: στῆθος 'chest' is the object of πλήξας, the aorist participle of πλήσσω 'strike', and κραδίην 'heart' the object of ἠνίπαπε. ἠνίπαπε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke'. Striking the chest is a gesture of self-rebuke. μύθῳ is 'with a word, a speech', and the colon brings in the speech that follows.

sentences.t: τέτλαθι δή, κραδίη·
sentences.tr: tetlathi dē, kradiē·
sentences.l: “Endure now, heart;
sentences.i: “Endure, now, my heart.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to his own heart. τέτλαθι is the perfect imperative of τλάω 'endure', a perfect that has the sense of a present, 'hold out, stay steady'. κραδίη is the vocative 'heart'. δή is a mild 'now, then'. The verb τλάω is rendered 'endure' throughout: it comes back in ἔτλης (next unit) and τετληυῖα (line 23), and its kin ἐτόλμας in line 20.
sentences.mark: Odysseus speaks to his own heart

sentences.t: καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο ποτ’ ἔτλης.
sentences.tr: kai kynteron allo pot’ etlēs.
sentences.l: even more dog-like another thing once you endured.
sentences.i: You once endured something even more shameless than this.
sentences.n: κύντερον is the comparative of κύων 'dog': 'more dog-like', hence more shameless or more brazen, and the word follows the dog of the simile just above. καί 'even'; ἄλλο 'another thing'; ποτ’ 'once, in the past'. ἔτλης is the aorist of τλάω. The thing endured is named in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε μοι μένος ἄσχετος ἤσθιε Κύκλωψ
ἰφθίμους ἑτάρους·
sentences.tr:
ēmati tōi hote moi menos aschetos ēsthie Kyklōps
iphthimous hetarous·
sentences.l:
On that day when unrestrained in fury the Cyclops was eating
my mighty companions;
sentences.i: That was the day when the Cyclops, unrestrained in his fury, was eating my mighty companions;
sentences.n: ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is 'on the day when'. μοι is a dative of interest, 'my'. ἄσχετος 'unrestrainable' is ἀ- 'not' + a verbal adjective of ἔχω 'hold'; μένος is both 'strength' and 'fury', here an accusative of respect, 'in fury'. ἤσθιε is the imperfect of ἐσθίω 'eat'. ἰφθίμους 'mighty' is a stock epithet of companions, rendered 'mighty' wherever it occurs; ἑτάρους is ἑταίρους, with the diphthong shortened.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐτόλμας, ὄφρα σε μῆτις
ἐξάγαγ’ ἐξ ἄντροιο ὀϊόμενον θανέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
sy d’ etolmas, ophra se mētis
exagag’ ex antroio oïomenon thaneesthai.
sentences.l:
but you bore it, until cunning
led you out of the cave, expecting to die.”
sentences.i: But you held out until cunning led you out of the cave, when you expected to die.”
sentences.n: ἐτόλμας is the imperfect of τολμάω 'have the heart to endure, hold out', a kin of τλάω. ὄφρα 'until' takes the aorist ἐξάγαγ’ (ἐξάγαγε, elided) of ἐξάγω 'lead out', and the subject is μῆτις 'cunning': Odysseus’s own cunning, not his strength, brought him out. σε and the participle ὀϊόμενον are masculine, because the heart he is addressing is also 'you', Odysseus himself; ὀϊόμενον is from ὀΐομαι 'suppose, expect', with θανέεσθαι, the future infinitive of θνῄσκω in its uncontracted form. The quotation closes.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἐν στήθεσσι καθαπτόμενος φίλον ἦτορ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, en stēthessi kathaptomenos philon ētor·
sentences.l: So he spoke, in his breast accosting his dear heart;
sentences.i: So he spoke, addressing his dear heart in his breast.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'So he spoke' (ἔφατο is the middle past of φημί), the same rendering as ὣς φάτο everywhere. καθαπτόμενος is 'accosting', from καθάπτομαι 'lay hold of; address'. φίλον ἦτορ is the fixed phrase 'dear heart': ἦτορ is another word for the heart, and here it names the same thing as κραδίη in the speech.

sentences.t:
τῷ δὲ μάλ’ ἐν πείσῃ κραδίη μένε τετληυῖα
νωλεμέως·
sentences.tr:
tōi de mal’ en peisēi kradiē mene tetlēuia
nōlemeōs·
sentences.l:
And to him wholly in obedience the heart remained, having endured
unceasingly;
sentences.i: And his heart stayed wholly obedient, enduring without pause;
sentences.n: τῷ is the dative of the pronoun, 'for him, his'. πείσῃ is a rare noun, 'obedience', from πείθομαι; ἐν πείσῃ μένε is 'stayed obedient'. τετληυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of τλάω, agreeing with κραδίη: 'having endured, enduring'. νωλεμέως 'unceasingly, without a break' is an adverb found only in verse. The heart obeys the order τέτλαθι.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ αὐτὸς ἑλίσσετο ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
sentences.tr: atar autos helisseto entha kai entha.
sentences.l: but he himself turned himself here and there.
sentences.i: but he himself kept turning this way and that.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ 'but' is a by-form of αὐτάρ. αὐτός 'he himself' sets Odysseus against the heart, which has just become still. ἑλίσσετο is the imperfect middle of ἑλίσσω 'turn', so 'was turning himself'. ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα 'here and there' is repeated in lines 26 and 28, where the turning becomes a simile.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε γαστέρ’ ἀνὴρ πολέος πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο,
ἐμπλείην κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος, ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
αἰόλλῃ, μάλα δ’ ὦκα λιλαίεται ὀπτηθῆναι,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote gaster’ anēr poleos pyros aithomenoio,
empleiēn knisēs te kai haimatos, entha kai entha
aiollēi, mala d’ ōka lilaietai optēthēnai,
sentences.l:
And as when a man a paunch over a great blazing fire,
full of fat and of blood, here and there
turns, and very quickly it longs to be roasted,
sentences.i: As when a man turns a paunch full of fat and blood this way and that over a great blazing fire, and it longs to be roasted very quickly,
sentences.n: A paunch is an animal’s stomach, stuffed, as here, with fat and blood and roasted whole. ὡς δ’ ὅτε 'as when' opens the simile. γαστέρ’ is the accusative of γαστήρ 'paunch'; ἐμπλείην is 'full', governing the genitives κνίσης 'fat' (the word usually means the savour of burning fat; here it is the fat itself) and αἵματος 'blood'. πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο is a genitive of place, 'over a burning fire', with the epic ending -οιο. αἰόλλῃ is a subjunctive of αἰόλλω 'turn quickly, shift'. λιλαίεται 'longs' and ὀπτηθῆναι, the aorist passive infinitive of ὀπτάω 'roast'. μάλα δ’ ὦκα, 'very quickly', could go with either verb. What is compared is the constant turning.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα ἑλίσσετο, μερμηρίζων
ὅππως δὴ μνηστῆρσιν ἀναιδέσι χεῖρας ἐφήσει
μοῦνος ἐὼν πολέσι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ho g’ entha kai entha helisseto, mermērizōn
hoppōs dē mnēstērsin anaidesi cheiras ephēsei
mounos eōn polesi.
sentences.l:
so then he here and there turned himself, pondering
how on the shameless suitors his hands he would lay,
being alone against many.
sentences.i: So he turned this way and that, pondering how he would lay hands on the shameless suitors, alone as he was against so many.
sentences.n: The simile is closed by ὣς ἄρ’ ὅ γε 'so then he'. μερμηρίζων 'pondering' is the verb that began the passage. ὅππως δή with the future ἐφήσει asks 'how he will …': ἐφίημι χεῖρας means 'lay hands on, attack'. ἀναιδέσι 'shameless' is the suitors' epithet here. μοῦνος ἐών is 'being alone' (Ionic μοῦνος for μόνος, ἐών for ὤν), and πολέσι the dative plural of πολύς 'many', with 'against' understood.

sentences.t:
σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ ἦλθεν Ἀθήνη
οὐρανόθεν καταβᾶσα·
sentences.tr:
schedothen de hoi ēlthen Athēnē
ouranothen katabasa·
sentences.l:
And near at hand came to him Athena,
from heaven having come down;
sentences.i: Athena came close to him, descending from the sky;
sentences.n: σχεδόθεν is 'from near, close by'; οἱ is 'to him'. οὐρανόθεν is 'from heaven', that is out of the sky: the suffix -θεν marks the place from which. καταβᾶσα is the aorist participle of καταβαίνω 'come down'.

sentences.t: δέμας δ’ ἤϊκτο γυναικί·
sentences.tr: demas d’ ēïkto gynaiki·
sentences.l: and in body she was likened to a woman;
sentences.i: and she took the likeness of a woman;
sentences.n: δέμας 'in body, in build' is an accusative of respect. ἤϊκτο is the pluperfect of ἔοικα, used as a past tense, 'was like', and it takes the dative γυναικί 'to a woman'. Athena comes in the shape of a woman, though in line 37 Odysseus calls her 'goddess' and so sees through it.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: stē d’ ar’ hyper kephalēs kai min pros mython eeipe·
sentences.l: and she stood then above his head, and to him spoke a word:
sentences.i: She stood over his head and spoke to him:
sentences.n: στῆ is ἔστη, the aorist of ἵστημι without the augment. ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς 'over his head' puts her at the head of the sleeper. μιν 'him'. πρὸς … ἔειπε is tmesis of προσεῖπον 'spoke to', with ἔειπε the epic aorist of εἶπον and μῦθον 'a word' as its object. The colon brings in her speech.

sentences.t: τίπτ’ αὖτ’ ἐγρήσσεις, πάντων περὶ κάμμορε φωτῶν;
sentences.tr: tipt’ aut’ egrēsseis, pantōn peri kammore phōtōn;
sentences.l: “Why again are you awake, beyond all, ill-fated one, of men?
sentences.i: “Why are you awake again, ill-fated beyond all other men?
sentences.n: Athena speaks. τίπτ’ is τίπτε, 'why ever' (τί ποτε). αὖτε 'again'. ἐγρήσσεις is 'are awake' (ἐγρήσσω, 'be awake, keep watch'). περί with the genitive πάντων … φωτῶν means 'beyond all men', and the vocative κάμμορε 'ill-fated one' stands in the middle of the phrase: κάμμορος is built on μόρος 'portion', 'ill-portioned'. φώς is the poetic word for 'man'.

sentences.t:
οἶκος μέν τοι ὅδ’ ἐστί, γυνὴ δέ τοι ἥδ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
καὶ, πάϊς, οἷόν πού τις ἐέλδεται ἔμμεναι υἷα.
sentences.tr:
oikos men toi hod’ esti, gynē de toi hēd’ eni oikōi
kai, païs, hoion pou tis eeldetai emmenai huia.
sentences.l:
A house, indeed, for you is this, and a wife for you is this in the house,
and a son, such as anyone, I suppose, wishes a son to be.”
sentences.i: This is your house, and in the house is this wife of yours, and a son too, such as anyone could wish his son to be.”
sentences.n: τοι is σοι 'for you', the enclitic dative of σύ; ὅδ’ and ἥδ’ are 'this' (ὅδε, ἥδε). The verb ἐστί stands once and serves for all three, house, wife and son. πάϊς is the nominative of παῖς 'child, son'. ἐέλδεται 'wishes, longs' takes the infinitive ἔμμεναι (= εἶναι) with the accusative υἷα (υἱός 'son'), and πού is 'I suppose, surely'. The quotation closes.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply, rendered with the same English every time. τὴν is 'her'; ἀπαμειβόμενος is 'answering'; προσέφη is 'addressed' (an aorist of πρόσφημι). πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is Odysseus’s stock epithet: μῆτις is 'cunning', so 'of many wiles'.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε πάντα, θεά, κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge panta, thea, kata moiran eeipes·
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, all these things, goddess, according to what is fitting you have said;
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, goddess, all this you have said as is fitting;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. ναί is 'yes', δή 'indeed', and γε stresses ταῦτα … πάντα 'all these things'. θεά is the vocative: Odysseus names her goddess, though she looks like a woman. κατὰ μοῖραν is 'according to what is fitting' (literally 'according to portion'), that is, 'rightly'. ἔειπες is the aorist 'you said'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τί μοι τόδε θυμὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μερμηρίζει,
ὅππως δὴ μνηστῆρσιν ἀναιδέσι χεῖρας ἐφήσω,
μοῦνος ἐών·
sentences.tr:
alla ti moi tode thymos eni phresi mermērizei,
hoppōs dē mnēstērsin anaidesi cheiras ephēsō,
mounos eōn·
sentences.i: but this is what my heart is pondering in my mind: how I am to lay hands on the shameless suitors, alone as I am;
sentences.n: Odysseus repeats the plan of lines 28–30, now in his own voice and in the first person: ἐφήσω 'I shall lay' where the narrator had ἐφήσει. τί is the indefinite 'something', so τί … τόδε is 'something like this'. θυμός 'heart' is the subject of μερμηρίζει, the verb that ran through the first lines. μοῦνος ἐών again 'being alone'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ αἰὲν ἀολλέες ἔνδον ἔασι.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ aien aollees endon easi.
sentences.l: but they ever, all together, within are.
sentences.i: and they are always inside, all together.
sentences.n: οἱ is 'they', the suitors, a pronoun. αἰέν is αἰεί 'always'. ἀολλέες is 'together, in a crowd', and ἔασι is the epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσί). The contrast with μοῦνος in the unit before is the whole difficulty.

sentences.t: πρὸς δ’ ἔτι καὶ τόδε μεῖζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μερμηρίζω·
sentences.tr: pros d’ eti kai tode meizon eni phresi mermērizō·
sentences.l: and besides, still also this, a greater thing, in my mind I ponder;
sentences.i: And besides, there is this still greater matter that I ponder in my mind:
sentences.n: πρός is an adverb here, 'besides, in addition'; ἔτι καί 'still also'; μεῖζον is the comparative of μέγας, 'greater'. μερμηρίζω is the first person of the verb that has run through the passage (lines 10, 28 and 38); here Odysseus uses it of himself. The greater matter follows.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γὰρ κτείναιμι Διός τε σέθεν τε ἕκητι,
πῆ κεν ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι;
sentences.tr:
ei per gar kteinaimi Dios te sethen te hekēti,
pē ken hypekprophygoimi;
sentences.l:
for if indeed I should kill, by the will of Zeus and of you,
whither could I escape?
sentences.i: For even if I kill them, by the will of Zeus and of yourself, where could I escape to?
sentences.n: εἴ περ is 'even if'. κτείναιμι is the aorist optative of κτείνω, a possible case ('if I were to kill'), and its object, the suitors, is left unsaid. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ. ἕκητι is a preposition with the genitive, 'by the will of, thanks to'. ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι is the aorist optative of ὑπεκπροφεύγω 'escape out from under'; with κεν it asks 'where could I get away to?'.

sentences.t: τά σε φράζεσθαι ἄνωγα.
sentences.tr: ta se phrazesthai anōga.
sentences.l: these things you to consider I bid.”
sentences.i: I bid you consider these things.”
sentences.n: τά is 'these things', the article used as a demonstrative pronoun. φράζεσθαι is the middle infinitive of φράζω 'consider, take thought of'. ἄνωγα is an old perfect with a present sense, 'I bid'; it takes the accusative and the infinitive, 'I bid you (σε) consider'. The quotation closes.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole-line formula of reply, with the same English every time. τὸν is 'him', αὖτε 'in turn', προσέειπε 'addressed'. γλαυκῶπις is Athena’s stock epithet, 'gleaming-eyed', rendered the same wherever it occurs.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιε, καὶ μέν τίς τε χερείονι πείθεθ’ ἑταίρῳ,
ὅς περ θνητός τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ τόσα μήδεα οἶδεν·
sentences.tr:
schetlie, kai men tis te chereioni peitheth’ hetairōi,
hos per thnētos t’ esti kai ou tosa mēdea oiden·
sentences.l:
“Cruel one, even someone trusts a worse companion,
who though mortal is, and not so many counsels knows;
sentences.i: “You cruel man, even a man will trust a worse companion, one who is only mortal and does not know so many counsels as I do;
sentences.n: Athena answers. σχέτλιε is a vocative of reproach, rendered 'cruel one' as everywhere: the word covers 'hard, enduring, cruel' and, in address, is nearer 'one who will not give up' than 'cruel', so she is chiding him for lying awake. καὶ μέν, 'even indeed', introduces a general truth, with τις 'someone' and the epic τε. πείθεθ’ is πείθεται, middle of πείθω, 'trusts' with the dative χερείονι ἑταίρῳ 'a worse companion' (χερείων is a comparative of κακός). ὅς περ 'who though'; θνητός 'mortal'. μήδεα 'counsels', with οὐ τόσα 'not so many'. The point is that she is a god.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ θεός εἰμι, διαμπερὲς ἥ σε φυλάσσω
ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοις.
sentences.tr:
autar egō theos eimi, diamperes hē se phylassō
en pantessi ponois.
sentences.l:
but I am a goddess, who continually guard you
in all labours.
sentences.i: But I am a goddess, and I guard you continually in all your labours.
sentences.n: θεός serves for a goddess as well as a god. The relative ἥ 'who' (accented) agrees with the speaker, so the verb is first person: 'I who guard you'. διαμπερές is 'all through, continually'. πάντεσσι is the dative plural of πᾶς in -εσσι, and πόνοις is 'labours, toils'.

sentences.t: ἐρέω δέ τοι ἐξαναφανδόν·
sentences.tr: ereō de toi exanaphandon·
sentences.l: and I will tell you openly:
sentences.i: And I will tell you plainly:
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future of λέγω, 'I will say'; τοι is σοι 'to you'. ἐξαναφανδόν is a long adverb, 'quite openly, plainly'.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ πεντήκοντα λόχοι μερόπων ἀνθρώπων
νῶϊ περισταῖεν, κτεῖναι μεμαῶτες Ἄρηϊ,
καί κεν τῶν ἐλάσαιο βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα.
sentences.tr:
ei per pentēkonta lochoi meropōn anthrōpōn
nōï peristaien, kteinai memaōtes Arēï,
kai ken tōn elasaio boas kai iphia mēla.
sentences.l:
even if fifty companies of speech-dividing men
were to stand around us two, eager to kill with Ares,
even so you could drive off their cattle and stout flocks.
sentences.i: Even if fifty companies of men of articulate speech were to stand round the two of us, eager to kill us in battle, you could still drive off their cattle and their stout flocks.
sentences.n: εἴ περ is 'even if'. λόχοι are 'companies', bands of fighting men (the word also means 'ambush'). The meaning of μέροπες in μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is not known: the ancient explanation, 'having divided speech', that is articulate, is followed here, and 'mortal' is the other common guess. νῶϊ is the dual 'us two', Athena and Odysseus. περισταῖεν is the aorist optative of περίστημι 'stand around'. κτεῖναι μεμαῶτες is 'eager to kill' (an aorist infinitive after the perfect participle of μέμαα 'strive'). Ἄρηϊ is the dative of Ares and stands for war, 'with Ares', that is in battle. καί κεν … ἐλάσαιο is 'even so you could drive off', an aorist optative middle of ἐλαύνω; τῶν is 'from them'. ἴφια μῆλα 'stout flocks'; μῆλα covers sheep and goats.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἑλέτω σε καὶ ὕπνος·
sentences.tr: all’ heletō se kai hypnos·
sentences.l: But let sleep take you too;
sentences.i: But now let sleep take you too;
sentences.n: ἑλέτω is the third-person aorist imperative of αἱρέω, 'let … take', and ὕπνος 'sleep' is its subject. καί is 'also, too'. The reason comes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἀνίη καὶ τὸ φυλάσσειν
πάννυχον ἐγρήσσοντα, κακῶν δ’ ὑποδύσεαι ἤδη.
sentences.tr:
aniē kai to phylassein
pannychon egrēssonta, kakōn d’ hypodyseai ēdē.
sentences.l:
irksome also is the keeping watch
all night awake, and from under evils you will slip out soon.”
sentences.i: To keep watch all night, awake, is tiresome too, and soon you will slip out from under your troubles.”
sentences.n: ἀνίη 'irksomeness' stands as a predicate, 'a tiresome thing'. τὸ φυλάσσειν is the infinitive 'the keeping watch' made into a noun by the article, and ἐγρήσσοντα 'being awake' agrees with an understood 'you'. πάννυχον 'all night long' is an adjective used as an adverb. κακῶν is a genitive with ὑποδύσεαι, the future of ὑποδύομαι 'slip out from under', in its uncontracted second singular form (Attic ὑποδύσῃ). ἤδη 'soon, now'. The quotation closes.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καί ῥά οἱ ὕπνον ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔχευεν,
αὐτὴ δ’ ἂψ ἐς Ὄλυμπον ἀφίκετο δῖα θεάων.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, kai rha hoi hypnon epi blepharoisin echeuen,
autē d’ aps es Olympon aphiketo dia theaōn.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and for him sleep upon the eyelids she poured,
and she herself back to Olympus came, heavenly-one of goddesses.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and poured sleep over his eyelids, and she herself, heavenly even among goddesses, went back to Olympus.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'So she spoke' (φάτο is ἔφατο without the augment), rendered like ὣς ἔφατ’ in lines 22 and 91. ῥά is a short form of ἄρα 'then'. οἱ 'for him'. ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν is 'upon the eyelids', and ἔχευεν 'poured', from χέω: sleep is poured on the eyelids like a liquid. αὐτή 'she herself'; ἂψ 'back'; ἀφίκετο 'arrived'. δῖα θεάων, 'heavenly even among goddesses', is the stock phrase for a goddess.

sentences.t:
εὖτε τὸν ὕπνος ἔμαρπτε, λύων μελεδήματα θυμοῦ,
λυσιμελής, ἄλοχος δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπέγρετο κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα·
sentences.tr:
eute ton hypnos emarpte, lyōn meledēmata thymou,
lysimelēs, alochos d’ ar’ epegreto kedna iduia·
sentences.l:
When him sleep was seizing, loosing the cares of his heart,
limb-loosening, his wife then awoke, the one wise and trusty;
sentences.i: As sleep took hold of him, loosing the cares of his heart and slackening his limbs, his wife woke, trusty and wise;
sentences.n: εὖτε is 'when, at the moment when'. ὕπνος is the subject of ἔμαρπτε, the imperfect of μάρπτω 'seize', with τὸν 'him' as object. λύων 'loosing' is joined by λυσιμελής 'limb-loosening' (λύω + μέλος 'limb'): sleep slackens the body. μελεδήματα 'cares'. ἄλοχος is 'wife'; the poet does not name her, but she is Penelope. ἐπέγρετο is the aorist middle of ἐπεγείρω 'wake'. κεδνὰ ἰδυῖα, 'trusty and wise', is a standing phrase of a loyal woman: ἰδυῖα is the perfect participle of οἶδα 'knowing'.

sentences.t: κλαῖε δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν λέκτροισι καθεζομένη μαλακοῖσιν.
sentences.tr: klaie d’ ar’ en lektroisi kathezomenē malakoisin.
sentences.l: and she wept then, in her soft bed seated.
sentences.i: and she wept, sitting up in her soft bed.
sentences.n: κλαῖε is the imperfect of κλαίω 'weep' and ἄρ’ is 'then'. λέκτροισι is the dative plural of λέκτρον 'bed'; as with στήθεσσι, the plural is poetic for one bed. καθεζομένη is 'sitting down', hence sitting up in bed. μαλακοῖσιν 'soft' has the dative plural in -οισιν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κλαίουσα κορέσσατο ὃν κατὰ θυμόν,
Ἀρτέμιδι πρώτιστον ἐπεύξατο δῖα γυναικῶν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei klaiousa koressato hon kata thymon,
Artemidi prōtiston epeuxato dia gynaikōn·
sentences.l:
But when, weeping, she had had her fill in her own heart,
to Artemis first of all she prayed, heavenly-one of women:
sentences.i: But when she had had her fill of weeping, in her own heart, she prayed first of all to Artemis, heavenly among women:
sentences.n: κορέσσατο is the aorist middle of κορέννυμι 'satisfy', 'had her fill', and the participle κλαίουσα 'weeping' says of what. ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is 'in her own heart': ὅς, ἥ, ὅν is here the possessive 'her own', not a relative. Ἀρτέμιδι is the dative of Ἄρτεμις. πρώτιστον 'first of all' is a superlative used as an adverb. ἐπεύξατο is 'prayed (to)'. δῖα γυναικῶν, 'heavenly among women', is Penelope’s stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Ἄρτεμι, πότνα θεά, θύγατερ Διός, αἴθε μοι ἤδη
ἰὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι βαλοῦσ’ ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιο
αὐτίκα νῦν,
sentences.tr:
Artemi, potna thea, thygater Dios, aithe moi ēdē
ion eni stēthessi balous’ ek thymon heloio
autika nyn,
sentences.l:
“Artemis, lady goddess, daughter of Zeus, would that now
an arrow into my breast having shot, my life out you would take
at once, now,
sentences.i: “Artemis, lady goddess, daughter of Zeus, if only you would shoot an arrow into my breast and take my life out of me, at once, this very moment,
sentences.n: Penelope prays for death. Ἄρτεμι and θύγατερ are vocatives, and πότνα θεά is 'lady goddess'. αἴθε introduces a wish, 'would that', with the optative ἕλοιο, 'you would take'; ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιο is tmesis, 'take out my life', and in this phrase θυμός is the life that leaves the body. βαλοῦσ’ is the aorist participle of βάλλω 'shoot', and ἰόν is 'arrow'. αὐτίκα νῦν is 'at once, now'. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἢ ἔπειτα μ’ ἀναρπάξασα θύελλα
οἴχοιτο προφέρουσα κατ’ ἠερόεντα κέλευθα,
ἐν προχοῇς δὲ βάλοι ἀψορρόου Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.tr:
ē epeita m’ anarpaxasa thyella
oichoito propherousa kat’ ēeroenta keleutha,
en prochoēis de baloi apsorroou Ōkeanoio.
sentences.l:
or then a storm-blast, snatching me up,
would go off carrying me forward along the misty paths,
and into the mouths would cast me of back-flowing Oceanus.
sentences.i: or else let a storm-blast then snatch me up and go off with me along the misty paths and throw me into the mouths of back-flowing Oceanus.
sentences.n: The optatives οἴχοιτο (οἴχομαι 'go off') and βάλοι continue the wish. ἀναρπάξασα is the aorist participle of ἀναρπάζω 'snatch up'; θύελλα is 'storm-blast'; προφέρουσα is 'carrying forward'. ἠερόεντα is 'misty' (from ἀήρ 'mist'), and κέλευθα 'ways, paths'. ἐν προχοῇς is 'into the mouths', the outflows (προχοαί, from προχέω 'pour out'). ἀψορρόου, from ἄψορρος 'flowing back', is an old epithet of Oceanus, the river that circles the world and so flows back into itself; that is the ancient explanation. Ὠκεανοῖο has the genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t: ὡς δ’ ὅτε Πανδαρέου κούρας ἀνέλοντο θύελλαι·
sentences.tr: hōs d’ hote Pandareou kouras anelonto thyellai·
sentences.l: As when Pandareus’ maidens the storm-blasts took up:
sentences.i: As when the storm-blasts carried off the daughters of Pandareus:
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε 'as when' opens a comparison with a story: she asks to be taken as Pandareus’ daughters were, and the story follows. κούρας is the accusative plural of κούρη 'maiden, daughter'; Πανδαρέου is the genitive in -έου. ἀνέλοντο is the aorist middle of ἀναιρέω 'take up, carry off'. θύελλαι is the plural of θύελλα 'storm-blast'.

sentences.t:
τῇσι τοκῆας μὲν φθῖσαν θεοί, αἱ δ’ ἐλίποντο
ὀρφαναὶ ἐν μεγάροισι, κόμισσε δὲ δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη
τυρῷ καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ καὶ ἡδέϊ οἴνῳ·
sentences.tr:
tēisi tokēas men phthisan theoi, hai d’ eliponto
orphanai en megaroisi, komisse de di’ Aphroditē
tyrōi kai meliti glykerōi kai hēdeï oinōi·
sentences.i: The gods destroyed their parents, and they were left orphans in the halls, and heavenly Aphrodite tended them with cheese and sweet honey and sweet wine;
sentences.n: τῇσι is the dative of the pronoun, 'to them', hence 'their'. τοκῆας 'parents' is the accusative plural of τοκεύς. φθῖσαν is the aorist of φθίω, here transitive, 'destroyed', without the augment. αἱ δέ 'but they'; ἐλίποντο 'were left' (middle of λείπω); ὀρφαναί 'orphans'. κόμισσε is the unaugmented aorist of κομίζω 'tend, take care of'. δῖ’ is δῖα 'heavenly'. The datives τυρῷ 'cheese', μέλιτι 'honey' and οἴνῳ 'wine' are of means; γλυκερῷ and ἡδέϊ both mean 'sweet'.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δ’ αὐτῇσιν περὶ πασέων δῶκε γυναικῶν
εἶδος καὶ πινυτήν, μῆκος δ’ ἔπορ’ Ἄρτεμις ἁγνή,
ἔργα δ’ Ἀθηναίη δέδαε κλυτὰ ἐργάζεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
Hērē d’ autēisin peri paseōn dōke gynaikōn
eidos kai pinytēn, mēkos d’ epor’ Artemis hagnē,
erga d’ Athēnaiē dedae klyta ergazesthai.
sentences.l:
And Hera gave to them, beyond all women,
beauty and discernment, and height gave Artemis the pure,
and works Athena taught them, famous ones, to work.
sentences.i: Hera gave them beauty and discernment beyond all other women, Artemis the pure gave them height, and Athena taught them to work famous works.
sentences.n: Ἥρη is Hera; αὐτῇσιν is the dative plural 'to them'; περὶ πασέων … γυναικῶν is 'beyond all women', with πασέων the epic genitive plural of πᾶς. εἶδος is 'beauty, form'. πινυτή is 'discernment', a noun related to πινυτός. μῆκος is 'length', hence height. ἔπορ’ is ἔπορε, the aorist of πόρω 'give'. ἁγνή is the stock epithet of Artemis, 'the pure'. δέδαε is a reduplicated aorist of δάω 'teach'. ἔργα κλυτά 'famous works' means skilled handiwork, the work of a woman’s hands. Four gods, four gifts.

sentences.t: εὖτ’ Ἀφροδίτη δῖα προσέστιχε μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
sentences.tr: eut’ Aphroditē dia prosestiche makron Olympon,
sentences.l: when heavenly Aphrodite went up to tall Olympus,
sentences.i: When heavenly Aphrodite went up to tall Olympus
sentences.n: The sentence opens with a long subordinate clause, interrupted by dashes, and its main clause comes in the unit after next. εὖτε 'when'; δῖα 'heavenly', agreeing with Ἀφροδίτη; προσέστιχε 'went up to'; μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον 'tall Olympus'.

sentences.t:
κούρῃς αἰτήσουσα τέλος θαλεροῖο γάμοιο—
ἐς Δία τερπικέραυνον, ὁ γάρ τ’ εὖ οἶδεν ἅπαντα,
sentences.tr:
kourēis aitēsousa telos thaleroio gamoio—
es Dia terpikeraunon, ho gar t’ eu oiden hapanta,
sentences.l:
to ask for the maidens the fulfilment of blooming marriage—
to bolt-delighting Zeus, for he well knows all things,
sentences.i: to ask for the maidens the fulfilment of a blooming marriage—to Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, for he knows all things well,
sentences.n: αἰτήσουσα is a future participle of purpose, 'to ask for'; κούρῃς is the dative 'for the maidens'; τέλος is 'fulfilment, accomplishment', here of a marriage, and θαλεροῖο 'blooming'. The dash opens the place she went: ἐς Δία τερπικέραυνον is 'to bolt-delighting Zeus', the house rendering, and ὁ γάρ τ’ means 'for he …', with the epic τε of a general truth.

sentences.t:
μοῖράν τ’ ἀμμορίην τε καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων—
τόφρα δὲ τὰς κούρας ἅρπυιαι ἀνηρείψαντο
καί ῥ’ ἔδοσαν στυγερῇσιν ἐρινύσιν ἀμφιπολεύειν·
sentences.tr:
moiran t’ ammoriēn te katathnētōn anthrōpōn—
tophra de tas kouras harpuiai anēreipsanto
kai rh’ edosan stygerēisin erinysin amphipoleuein·
sentences.i: both the portion and the lack of portion of mortal men—meanwhile the Harpies carried off the maidens and gave them to the hateful Erinyes to wait on;
sentences.n: μοῖρα and ἀμμορίη, 'portion' and 'lack of portion', stand for what is allotted to mortal men and what is not, their good and ill fortune; καταθνητῶν 'mortal'. The dash closes the aside, and τόφρα δέ, 'but meanwhile', answers εὖτε in line 73. ἅρπυιαι, which Murray prints with a small letter, are the Harpies, 'snatchers' (ἁρπάζω), storm-winds personified; in English they take a capital. ἀνηρείψαντο is the aorist middle of ἀνερείπομαι 'snatch away'. ῥ’ is ῥά, 'then'. στυγερῇσιν is the dative plural 'hateful'. ἐρινύσιν is the dative plural of Ἐρινύς, an Erinys, one of the goddesses who avenge wrongs. ἀμφιπολεύειν, 'to wait on, serve', is an infinitive of purpose.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔμ’ ἀϊστώσειαν Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες,
ἠέ μ’ ἐϋπλόκαμος βάλοι Ἄρτεμις, ὄφρ’ Ὀδυσῆα
ὀσσομένη καὶ γαῖαν ὕπο στυγερὴν ἀφικοίμην,
μηδέ τι χείρονος ἀνδρὸς ἐϋφραίνοιμι νόημα.
sentences.tr:
hōs em’ aïstōseian Olympia dōmat’ echontes,
ēe m’ eÿplokamos baloi Artemis, ophr’ Odysēa
ossomenē kai gaian hypo stygerēn aphikoimēn,
mēde ti cheironos andros eÿphrainoimi noēma.
sentences.l:
So may those who hold the Olympian halls make me vanish,
or may fine-plaited Artemis strike me, so that, Odysseus
picturing, even beneath the hateful earth I might come,
and not at all of a worse man gladden the mind.
sentences.i: So may those who hold the halls of Olympus make me vanish, or may fine-plaited Artemis strike me down, so that with Odysseus before my eyes I may go even beneath the hateful earth, and never gladden the mind of a worse man.
sentences.n: ὣς 'so, in this way' answers the ὡς δ’ ὅτε of line 66: let it be done to her as to those maidens. ἀϊστώσειαν is the aorist optative of ἀϊστόω 'make unseen, make vanish'. Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες, 'those who hold the Olympian halls', is a periphrasis for the gods. ἐϋπλόκαμος is 'fine-plaited', the word used of Calypso, here of Artemis. ὄφρα with the optative ἀφικοίμην is 'so that I might arrive'. ὀσσομένη, from ὄσσομαι (compare ὄσσε 'eyes'), is 'having him before her eyes, picturing him'; Ὀδυσῆα is the accusative, beside Ὀδυσσῆα. γαῖαν ὕπο has the preposition after its noun. ἐϋφραίνοιμι, 'I might gladden', still depends on ὄφρα, and χείρονος is the comparative of κακός, 'worse': the context shows the worse man is a second husband.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν καὶ ἀνεκτὸν ἔχει κακόν, ὁππότε κέν τις
ἤματα μὲν κλαίῃ, πυκινῶς ἀκαχήμενος ἦτορ,
sentences.tr:
alla to men kai anekton echei kakon, hoppote ken tis
ēmata men klaiēi, pykinōs akachēmenos ētor,
sentences.l:
But that, indeed, even bearable holds the evil, whenever anyone
by days weeps, thickly grieved in heart,
sentences.i: But that is an evil one can even bear, whenever someone weeps through the days, sorely grieved at heart,
sentences.n: The general case comes first, and the point is made at line 87. τὸ μὲν … ἔχει κακόν is 'that holds an evil that is even bearable': τό is the subject, the state described in what follows, and ἀνεκτόν goes with κακόν. ὁππότε κέν τις 'whenever anyone' takes the subjunctive κλαίῃ 'weeps' (and ἔχῃσιν in the next unit); ἤματα, 'by days', is an accusative of time. ἀκαχήμενος ἦτορ is 'grieved in heart', the heart an accusative of respect, and πυκινῶς, 'thickly', means heavily.

sentences.t:
νύκτας δ’ ὕπνος ἔχῃσιν—ὁ γάρ τ’ ἐπέλησεν ἁπάντων,
ἐσθλῶν ἠδὲ κακῶν, ἐπεὶ ἄρ βλέφαρ’ ἀμφικαλύψῃ—
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ καὶ ὀνείρατ’ ἐπέσσευεν κακὰ δαίμων.
sentences.tr:
nyktas d’ hypnos echēisin—ho gar t’ epelēsen hapantōn,
esthlōn ēde kakōn, epei ar blephar’ amphikalypsēi—
autar emoi kai oneirat’ epesseuen kaka daimōn.
sentences.l:
and by nights sleep holds him—for it makes him forget all things,
good and bad, when it has covered his eyelids around—
but against me even dreams drove evil, some power.
sentences.i: and sleep holds him through the nights—for sleep makes him forget everything, good and bad alike, once it has covered his eyelids over—but some power has driven even evil dreams upon me.
sentences.n: νύκτας, 'by nights', is an accusative of time and ἔχῃσιν the second subjunctive after ὁππότε κέν. In the dashes ὁ is a pronoun, 'it' (sleep), and the τε of ὁ γάρ τ’ marks a general truth. ἐπέλησεν is the aorist of ἐπιλήθω 'make forget', with the genitive ἁπάντων 'of all things'. ἀμφικαλύψῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἀμφικαλύπτω 'cover around'. αὐτάρ 'but' turns the argument: ordinarily sleep brings forgetfulness, but for her it brings dreams. ὀνείρατ’ is ὀνείρατα 'dreams', and κακά 'evil' goes with it. ἐπέσσευεν is a past tense (the aorist) of ἐπισεύω 'urge on, drive at', with the σ doubled for the metre. δαίμων is 'some power', an unnamed divine force.

sentences.t:
τῇδε γὰρ αὖ μοι νυκτὶ παρέδραθεν εἴκελος αὐτῷ,
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷος ᾖεν ἅμα στρατῷ·
sentences.tr:
tēide gar au moi nykti paredrathen eikelos autōi,
toios eōn hoios ēien hama stratōi·
sentences.l:
For this night again beside me slept one like to him himself,
such being as he was when he went with the army;
sentences.i: For again this night someone lay beside me, the very likeness of him, such as he was when he went off with the army;
sentences.n: τῇδε … νυκτί is 'this night', a dative of time, and αὖ 'again'. The subject of παρέδραθεν, the aorist of παραδαρθάνω 'sleep beside', is not named: it is a figure that looked like Odysseus. εἴκελος is 'like', with the dative αὐτῷ 'to himself', that is to Odysseus in person. τοῖος ἐών οἷος … is 'being such as …'; ᾖεν is ᾔει, the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', and ἅμα takes the dative στρατῷ 'with the army'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὸν κῆρ
χαῖρ’, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐφάμην ὄναρ ἔμμεναι, ἀλλ’ ὕπαρ ἤδη.
sentences.tr:
autar emon kēr
chair’, epei ouk ephamēn onar emmenai, all’ hypar ēdē.
sentences.l:
and my heart
rejoiced, since I did not say it was a dream, but now a waking sight.”
sentences.i: and my heart rejoiced, for I did not suppose it was a dream, but already a waking sight.”
sentences.n: κῆρ is another word for the heart, and it is the subject of χαῖρ’, the imperfect of χαίρω 'rejoice'. ἐφάμην is the imperfect of φημί, 'I said', which the English layer takes as 'I supposed' because what she reports is her own thought. ὄναρ is 'dream' and ὕπαρ 'waking sight', a thing seen awake; ἔμμεναι is εἶναι. ἤδη is 'now, already'. The prayer ends here and the quotation closes.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτίκα δὲ χρυσόθρονος ἤλυθεν Ἠώς.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autika de chrysothronos ēlythen Ēōs.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and golden-throned Dawn came at once.
sentences.n: The narrator closes the speech and brings in the morning. ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'So she spoke'; αὐτίκα 'at once'; ἤλυθεν is the aorist of ἔρχομαι, 'came'. χρυσόθρονος, 'golden-throned', is the stock epithet of Dawn; an old alternative derives the second half from θρόνα 'embroidered flowers', so that the sense would be 'of the golden flowers'.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ ἄρα κλαιούσης ὄπα σύνθετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēs d’ ara klaiousēs opa syntheto dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: And of her weeping the voice took in heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: And heavenly Odysseus heard the voice of her weeping;
sentences.n: τῆς is 'her'; κλαιούσης is the genitive participle 'weeping', and ὄπα the accusative of ὄψ 'voice'. σύνθετο is the aorist middle of συντίθημι 'put together', that is 'take in, grasp what he heard', with the genitive of the person and the accusative of the sound. ἄρα is 'then'. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is again 'heavenly Odysseus'.

sentences.t:
μερμήριζε δ’ ἔπειτα, δόκησε δέ οἱ κατὰ θυμὸν
ἤδη γιγνώσκουσα παρεστάμεναι κεφαλῆφι.
sentences.tr:
mermērize d’ epeita, dokēse de hoi kata thymon
ēdē gignōskousa parestamenai kephalēphi.
sentences.l:
and he pondered then, and it seemed to him in heart
that already recognising him she stood by his head.
sentences.i: Then he pondered, and in his heart it seemed to him that she already recognised him and was standing at his head.
sentences.n: μερμήριζε 'pondered' is the verb of lines 10, 28 and 38 again. δόκησε is the aorist of δοκέω 'seem', with οἱ 'to him'. The construction is personal: γιγνώσκουσα is feminine nominative, so the sentence is 'she seemed to him, already recognising him, to be standing nearby'. παρεστάμεναι is the infinitive of παρίστημι in -άμεναι (compare ἔμμεναι). κεφαλῆφι 'at his head' has the suffix -φι of place.

sentences.t:
χλαῖναν μὲν συνελὼν καὶ κώεα, τοῖσιν ἐνεῦδεν,
ἐς μέγαρον κατέθηκεν ἐπὶ θρόνου, ἐκ δὲ βοείην
θῆκε θύραζε φέρων, Διὶ δ’ εὔξατο χεῖρας ἀνασχών·
sentences.tr:
chlainan men synelōn kai kōea, toisin eneuden,
es megaron katethēken epi thronou, ek de boeiēn
thēke thyraze pherōn, Dii d’ euxato cheiras anaschōn·
sentences.l:
The cloak indeed having gathered up, and the fleeces on which he had slept,
into the hall he set down on a chair, and out the oxhide
he put, carrying it out of doors, and to Zeus he prayed, his hands raising:
sentences.i: He gathered up the cloak and the fleeces he had been sleeping on, set them down in the hall on a chair, and carried the oxhide outside; and he prayed to Zeus, raising his hands:
sentences.n: μέν marks the first of two contrasted actions: cloak and fleeces taken in, hide taken out (ἐκ δέ). συνελών is the aorist participle of συναιρέω 'gather together'. τοῖσιν … ἐνεῦδεν: τοῖσιν is a relative, 'on which', and ἐνεῦδεν the imperfect of ἐνεύδω 'sleep in'. ἐς μέγαρον is 'into the hall', and κατέθηκεν 'set down'; ἐπὶ θρόνου is 'on a chair'. ἐκ … θῆκε is tmesis, 'put out'; βοείην is the oxhide of line 2; θύραζε 'out of doors' has the suffix -ζε of direction; φέρων 'carrying'. Διὶ … εὔξατο: εὔχομαι with the dative is 'pray to'. χεῖρας ἀνασχών, 'raising his hands', is the gesture of prayer. The prayer itself begins in the next part.
